title: Competing rationales for major questions review
shortTitle: Competing rationales for major questions review
summary: The assigned opinions disagree whether major questions review protects a constitutional allocation of power, draws a contextual inference about delegation, or improperly narrows broad statutory language.
notes:
Justice Gorsuch’s West Virginia concurrence, summarized in the notes, treats the doctrine as a clear-statement principle supporting Article I’s placement of legislative power in Congress. He links it to nondelegation and to narrow constructions that avoid constitutionally doubtful transfers of power. The authors ask whether that logic should make its reach track the underlying nondelegation concern, including Gorsuch’s attention to coercion of private conduct. They ask how a benefits case such as student loan relief fits that account. Those are editorial questions, not answers supplied by the concurrence. (Printed 982.)

Justice Barrett’s Biden v. Nebraska concurrence gives a different explanation. She treats the scale of the delegation as part of ordinary communicative context: what would a principal reasonably be understood to authorize an agent to do? She expresses concern about strong substantive canons that displace a statute’s natural meaning. Constitutional structure is part of context in her approach, while a separate clear-statement rule to enforce nondelegation goes further than her justification. (Printed 982–983.)

Justice Kagan’s West Virginia dissent argues that broad language can deliberately enable important regulatory action in response to unforeseen problems. On her reading, the earlier cases involved mismatches between agency expertise, claimed power, and statutory structure. EPA’s regulation of power-plant pollution presented no comparable mismatch. She therefore objects to a separate clear-authorization hurdle. The majority instead reads the same precedents as a distinct approach for extraordinary assertions of power. A careful analysis identifies the precise claimed delegation and evaluates how each rationale treats it. (Printed 973–980.)
